how-much-to-charge-to-replace-a-sliding-.text:
← Patio door bid calculator

How much to charge to replace a sliding glass door

The number a homeowner wants is a published “$1,800 installed” 6-foot vinyl 2-panel special, or a “$400 to swap a slider” coupon. That number is not a takeoff. A 6-foot vinyl retrofit on a ground patio is not the same job as a 16-foot 4-panel impact-rated new-construction unit with a transom, a new sill pan, and second-story balcony access. The trip is the same. The hours are not.

Open the free bid calculator

Count the panels and the extras, not just “a patio door”

Entry-door calculators price sidelights, jamb rot, and a storm door. Window-replacement calculators price united inches and flashing. A sliding or patio-door hang is a different job: the panels, the glass, the install method, and the extras that are not in the coupon. Quoting all of that from a published installed special is how the first sill-pan rebuild eats the field margin.

A job with the same trip can cost much more

Each extra panel is time and glass that never appears on the coupon. Impact glass, a full-frame wrap, a transom, a sill pan, and balcony access are billed as their own hours. On the sample rates a 16-foot 4-panel fiberglass unit with impact glass, new-construction wrap, transom, sill pan, threshold rebuild, screen, interior trim, tear-out, and balcony access prices about $23,344.28 (32.6 crew-hours). The same shop’s 6-foot vinyl brochure hang prices about $2,770.12 (7.4 hours, walk-away $1,883.68). Matching the brochure job’s $1,800 special on the 4-panel house is how that job becomes a loss — the walk-away on the heavy job is already $15,874.11, and the $1,800 special loses about $14,074 there. The $1,800 special loses $83.68 even on the brochure hang.

Triple-pane and a 3-panel hang are not automatically a markup on vinyl

A 12-foot 3-panel vinyl hang with triple-pane glass, new-construction wrap, screen, interior trim, and a sill pan is not the 6-foot brochure hang plus 15%. On the sample rates that 3-panel job prices about $7,975.38 (22.2 crew-hours). A retrofit pocket drops wrap hours; extra panels and impact glass do not disappear with the pocket. Treating either as a blended add-on is how the special that looked fine turns into a loss after the first sill-pan rebuild.

Load the wage, then keep a walk-away number

A $48/h installer loaded at 32% payroll burden is $63.36. Margin is a share of the price you send, not a markup on cost. The walk-away price is total cost — below that the job makes nothing before you take a dollar home. Replace every rate with your invoices before you send either number.

What this is not

This is not a door design, a building-code determination, a permit, an engineering stamp, or a recommended market price. It is arithmetic on the numbers you type. The opening, the unit, glass, install method, flashing, and trim are yours to confirm. It does not price a pedestrian entry door or a window replacement.

Price your patio-door hang

Common questions

How much to charge to replace a sliding glass door?

Charge from the trip, the set, extra panels, glass (dual, triple, or impact), install method (retrofit pocket versus new-construction wrap), balcony access, screen, transom, interior trim, sill pan, loaded labor, overhead, and a margin that is a share of price. A default 6-foot vinyl 2-panel retrofit on a ground patio, at the sample rates in this calculator, prices around $2,770 — about 7.4 crew-hours.

Why is a $1,800-installed patio-door special dangerous?

Homeowners count a patio door. Extra panels, impact glass, a full-frame wrap, a transom, a sill pan, and a balcony do not scale with that number. Matching a cheaper special written for a 6-foot vinyl hang is how a 4-panel impact balcony job becomes a two-day loss. On the sample rates the $1,800 special already loses about $84 on the brochure hang (walk-away $1,884) and loses about $14,074 on the 4-panel house whose walk-away is already $15,874.

How much to charge to replace a 4-panel impact sliding door?

A 16-foot 4-panel fiberglass unit with impact glass, new-construction wrap, transom, sill pan, and balcony access is not a 6-foot vinyl special. On the sample rates that job prices around $23,344 (32.6 crew-hours), while a 6-foot vinyl brochure hang prices around $2,770 (7.4 hours).

      Why is a balcony unit priced so much higher than the same door on a ground patio?

vs-a-flat-installed-price.html.text:
← Patio Door Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat "$1,800 installed" patio door special

"$1,800 patio door installed" is not a price for a patio door install — it is a price for one 6-foot vinyl 2-panel retrofit hang, quietly applied to every opening the truck pulls up to.

What a flat "$1,800 installed" special is

A flat special is the fastest way to quote: one headline number on a postcard or a website, read off and repeated. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number a customer holding a competitor's flyer will ask you to match on their own opening.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually the cheapest configuration (a vinyl retrofit hang, dual-pane glass, at grade, no new-construction wrap, no transom, no sill pan) — and then reused for every patio door afterward, whether or not the next opening looks anything like that hang.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the panel configuration, frame material, glazing, whether the install is a retrofit into an existing frame or a full new-construction wrap, ground or balcony access, extras such as a screen, a transom, interior trim, a sill pan, and a threshold rebuild, and your loaded labor and overhead. It prices the set labor, the wrap, the access, and the extras separately, and returns a walk-away price for the job you describe — for this opening, not a generic one.

Worked using this calculator's own starting kits and job presets at a $48 crew wage, 32% payroll burden, 16% overhead on direct cost, and a 32% target margin — the form's own defaults, not a number invented for this page. Open the calculator's presets to check any row yourself.

What a flat special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same headline price whether the job is a 6-foot vinyl retrofit hang or a 16-foot fiberglass new-construction unit with impact glass and balcony access — several times the labor and material for the same words "patio door". Prices the panels, frame, and glazing from the entered configuration, so jobs of different scope come out at different numbers instead of one.
Prices "a patio door" as one drop-in swap, with no separate line for a full-frame new-construction wrap, a new sill pan, or hoisting panels to a second-story balcony. Times the wrap, the sill pan, and the balcony access as their own extra-work hours, so that work shows up instead of being absorbed into the sash price or skipped.
Assumes dual-pane glass and a vinyl frame, so triple-pane, impact glazing, aluminum, fiberglass, or wood-clad frames get quoted the same as the cheapest option. Applies a glazing cost factor and a frame unit cost only for what was entered, so heavier frames and upgraded glass price differently.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "labor rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the crew a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a homeowner asks to match a cheaper flat rate on a bigger opening. Reports a walk-away price built from the entered scope, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the crew commits to it.

A flat special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat "$1,800 installed" patio-door special get the price wrong?

Because the labor and material scale with the panel count, frame, glazing, install method, and access, not with the phrase "patio door" alone. A 6-foot vinyl 2-panel retrofit into an existing frame at grade is a different job from a 16-foot fiberglass 4-panel unit with impact glass, a new-construction wrap, a transom, a sill pan, and second-story balcony access. A flat special quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat special usually leave out entirely?

The frame, the glazing upgrade, the new-construction wrap, and the access. A published installed price is set on the cheapest configuration — a vinyl retrofit hang, dual-pane glass, at grade — and has nowhere to put the hours and material for a heavier frame, impact or triple-pane glass, a full-frame wrap with a new sill pan, a transom, or hoisting panels to a second-story balcony. A shop pricing off the special alone is short before the crew unloads the truck.

How much do the frame, glazing, and access actually add over the flat special?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $48 crew wage, 32% burden, 16% overhead, and a 32% target margin: even the cheapest job it prices — a 6-foot vinyl 2-panel retrofit at grade with a tear-out — walks away at $2,770.12, already $970.12 over the $1,800 special. A 12-foot 3-panel vinyl unit with triple-pane glass, a new-construction wrap, a screen, and a sill pan walks away at $7,975.38, over $6,175 over the special. A 16-foot 4-panel fiberglass unit with impact glass, a full new-construction wrap, a transom, a sill pan, and balcony access walks away at $23,344.28, over $21,500 over the special. The frame, the glazing, the wrap, and the access — not the word "patio door" — are what move the number.

Is a flat rate ever the right way to quote a patio door?

For the one job it was actually priced on it can land close, but on this calculator's own defaults even that cheapest job — a 6-foot vinyl 2-panel retrofit at grade — already clears $1,800 once real payroll burden, overhead, and a target margin are applied. A flat special set years ago, or set without those loaded costs, keeps quoting a number the shop's own arithmetic no longer supports, and the gap only grows on anything bigger than the base hang.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates, permit fees, or what competitors charge. It takes the panel configuration, frame, glazing, install method, access, extras, and your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat "$1,800 installed" special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

← Patio Door Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. Jobber

Two different shapes: Jobber is account-based field-service software for running a home-service business across clients, scheduling, and crews. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this patio-door job cost, given its panels, frame, glazing, and access, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

Jobber is field-service management software founded in 2011 and headquartered in Edmonton, Alberta, Canada, used by home-service businesses across HVAC, plumbing, electrical, lawn care, and cleaning trades. It combines client management, quoting, scheduling, invoicing, and payment collection into one subscription system meant to run a whole business across every job and every crew, and it says it serves over 200,000 users. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. Jobber's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — home-service field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for Jobber appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what Jobber does. It does not manage clients, schedule crews, send invoices, or collect payments, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes the panel configuration (2, 3, or 4 panels), frame material, glazing, retrofit-versus-new-construction install method, ground-versus-balcony access, and extras like a screen, transom, interior trim, sill pan, or threshold rebuild, plus loaded wage, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the walk-away price below which the job loses money, a breakdown of where the hours and cost actually go, and a copyable customer-facing bid summary — plus a printable customer proposal with scope lines and a signature block. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.
